rows: UKHSA leads national work on antimicrobial resistance through surveillance, microbiology, research and evidence-based interventions.
AMR capabilities include pathogen genomics, epidemiology, modelling and antimicrobial stewardship.
UKHSA's AMR and HCAI division supports prevention of healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial resistance.
Outbreak response includes prompt risk assessment and specialist pathogen identification.
Unusual antimicrobial resistance of public-health importance can trigger therapeutic guidance and enhanced investigation.
Research programmes develop and monitor infection-prevention and antimicrobial-stewardship interventions.
UKHSA work aligns with the UK's 2024 to 2029 antimicrobial-resistance National Action Plan.
The programme uses a One Health approach spanning human, animal and environmental sectors.
National AMR surveillance does not demonstrate a resistant organism or outbreak at a specific property.
Local conclusions require current organism, susceptibility, patient, facility and outbreak-investigation evidence.
The FSA identifies bacteria and viruses including Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and norovirus as causes of food poisoning.
Correct cooking time and temperature are central food-poisoning controls.
Chilling food below 5°C stops or significantly slows bacterial growth.
Cleaning food-contact equipment and surfaces helps prevent harmful organisms spreading to food.
Separating raw and ready-to-eat foods reduces cross-contamination.
Food should not be eaten after its use-by date even where it looks or smells acceptable.
Good personal hygiene is essential during food preparation.
Suspected food poisoning or food-safety problems can be reported to the relevant local authority.
General food-poisoning guidance does not prove contamination at a particular food business or home.
A local conclusion requires product, meal, symptom, laboratory, inspection and epidemiological evidence.
Listeria monocytogenes control is particularly important for chilled ready-to-eat food served to vulnerable people.
Cleaning food-contact surfaces is a core Listeria control.
Managing cross-contamination is an essential food-safety control for Listeria.
Controls should minimise growth of Listeria in chilled ready-to-eat foods.
Businesses should apply effective food-safety controls across preparation, storage and service.
Older people and other vulnerable consumers face a greater risk of serious illness from listeriosis.
FSA advice highlights risk associated with ready-to-eat cold-smoked and cured fish for higher-risk consumers.
Supplier assurance and implementation checks support effective Listeria risk management.
A food category or premises type does not prove Listeria contamination or control failure.
Local conclusions require current product, batch, temperature, hygiene, sampling and traceability evidence.
Salmonella is a group of bacteria that can cause food poisoning.
Thorough cooking reduces Salmonella risk in raw meat and poultry products.
Handwashing after handling uncooked food helps prevent transfer to ready-to-eat food.
Preparation surfaces and utensils should be cleaned after contact with uncooked products.
FSA advice has highlighted care when preparing lamb, mutton and other raw meat during Salmonella investigations.
Frozen part-cooked breaded poultry must be cooked according to instructions because it may appear pre-cooked.
Raw and cooked foods should be kept separate to reduce cross-contamination.
Good kitchen hygiene and adequate cooking significantly reduce risks from Salmonella and E. coli.
A general advisory or product category does not prove that a specific food item is contaminated.
Product-level conclusions require batch, origin, cooking, sampling, recall and epidemiological evidence.
